problem: The sentence says the lining wears fastest where pressure × sliding speed is largest, 'which is at the inner radius'. Sliding speed is ωr, so pressure × sliding speed grows with radius. A new, nearly uniformly loaded face wears fastest at the OUTER radius. That is exactly why the face redistributes until p × r is constant, leaving the highest pressure at the inner radius. The sentence also contradicts the chapter's own Quiz Q2 answer, so a student gets two opposite statements.
fix: Rewrite as: 'A new clutch has pressure nearly uniform over the face. Wear rate goes as pressure × sliding speed, and sliding speed is ωr, so the outer lining wears fastest. After running in, the face settles into a state where pressure × radius is constant — uniform wear — and the highest pressure then sits at r_i, the smallest radius.'

where: Worked example 1, step 9 (and the answer 11.8 kJ)
problem: Step 9 says 'the torque falls from its peak to zero as the speeds equalise'. Under a constant spring force the friction torque stays roughly constant; it is the relative speed Δω that falls from 600 rpm to zero. With constant torque the fall in Δω is linear, so the mean Δω is Δω₀/2 and the heat per engagement is about half the quoted value. The stated 11.8 kJ is therefore roughly double the correct estimate, and the reason given for calling it an estimate is wrong.
fix: Step 9: 'The friction torque stays roughly constant, but the relative speed falls linearly from 600 rpm to zero, so the mean relative speed is half the initial value. E ≈ T (Δω/2) t = 375 × 31.4 × 0.5 ≈ 5890 J.' Answer: 'about 5.9 kJ per engagement'. Keep E = T Δω t only for steady slipping, as in a brake holding a constant speed.

problem: Section 1 says 'p plates give p − 1 rubbing pairs', which read literally gives zero pairs for a single-plate clutch, while Section 2 and the example say a single-plate clutch has n = 2 rubbing pairs. The p − 1 rule only holds when the flywheel and pressure-plate faces are counted as plates too.
fix: Add one clarifying clause: 'Count every friction surface, including the flywheel face and the pressure-plate face. A stack of p such members gives p − 1 rubbing pairs; the familiar single plate lined on both faces, clamped between flywheel and pressure plate, is three members and so gives 2 pairs.'
